LIN-TIME-SYNC.why: Unsynchronized time breaks reliable event ordering, certificate validation, and time-sensitive authentication such as Kerberos. Attackers benefit when defenders cannot accurately correlate activity across hosts or when authentication failures create operational confusion.

test.label: Check common time-synchronization services
test.cmd: systemctl is-active chronyd systemd-timesyncd ntp ntpd 2>/dev/null

fix.label: Enable an approved time service
fix.text: Configure and enable chronyd, systemd-timesyncd, or ntpd with approved redundant time sources, then confirm the clock reports synchronized.

LIN-BOOT-SECUREBOOT.title: UEFI Secure Boot
LIN-BOOT-SECUREBOOT.semantics: PASS: Secure Boot enabled; WARN: UEFI with Secure Boot disabled; INFO: legacy BIOS boot.
LIN-BOOT-SECUREBOOT.why: UEFI Secure Boot helps prevent untrusted bootloaders and kernels from running before operating-system defenses are active. If it is disabled on a UEFI system, an attacker with administrative or physical write access can establish pre-OS persistence that is difficult to detect.

test.label: Determine firmware boot mode
test.cmd: if [ -d /sys/firmware/efi ]; then echo UEFI; else echo legacy-BIOS; fi

fix.label: Enable UEFI Secure Boot
fix.text: Verify that the bootloader, kernel, and required drivers are signed and compatible, then enable Secure Boot in the system firmware and protect firmware configuration from unauthorized changes.

LIN-SVC-FAILED.title: Failed systemd units
LIN-SVC-FAILED.why: Failed systemd units can indicate disabled security controls, broken monitoring, incomplete patching, or an unstable service dependency. Attackers may benefit when a firewall, audit agent, authentication service, or other protective component has silently failed.

fix.label: Investigate each failed unit
fix.text: Review systemctl status and journalctl -u output for every failed unit, repair its configuration or dependency, and only disable the unit if its removal is intentional and documented.

LIN-CTR-DOCKERSOCK.title: Docker socket exposure
LIN-CTR-DOCKERSOCK.semantics: FAIL: /var/run/docker.sock world-writable or writable by the current non-root user; PASS: present and restricted; NA: absent.
LIN-CTR-DOCKERSOCK.why: Write access to the Docker daemon socket is effectively root-equivalent because the daemon can create privileged containers and mount the host filesystem. An attacker who can write to the socket can escape normal account restrictions and take over the host.

test.label: Inspect Docker socket ownership and mode
Test current-user write access
test.cmd: if [ -S /var/run/docker.sock ]; then if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ] && [ -w /var/run/docker.sock ]; then echo 'writable by current non-root user'; else echo 'not writable by current non-root user'; fi; else echo 'socket absent'; fi

fix.label: Restrict Docker daemon access
fix.text: Remove unauthorized users from the docker group, ensure the socket is not world-writable, and grant daemon access only to accounts treated as root-equivalent; consider rootless Docker where operationally suitable.

LIN-AD-JOINED.title: Directory membership
LIN-AD-JOINED.semantics: INFO: realm/sssd/winbind membership and realm name, or not joined.
LIN-AD-JOINED.why: Directory-membership inventory identifies whether authentication and authorization depend on an external realm, SSSD, or winbind. Attackers who compromise domain credentials or trust configuration may gain access across multiple joined hosts, while unexpected membership can reveal unauthorized enrollment.

test.label: Show configured SSSD or winbind domains

fix.label: Validate directory membership
fix.text: Confirm every reported realm against the approved asset and identity design; remove obsolete membership through the platform's supported realm-leave process only after arranging replacement authentication and recovery access.

LIN-AD-KEYTAB.title: Host keytab readability
LIN-AD-KEYTAB.semantics: FAIL: /etc/krb5.keytab readable by the current non-root user or world-readable; PASS: present and restricted; NA: absent.
LIN-AD-KEYTAB.why: A Kerberos host keytab contains long-term keys used to authenticate the machine or its services. A non-root attacker who can read it may impersonate principals, request tickets, or move laterally within the trusted realm.

test.label: Test non-root readability without displaying keys
test.cmd: if [ ! -e /etc/krb5.keytab ]; then echo 'keytab absent'; elif [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then echo 'run this readability test as a non-root user'; elif [ -r /etc/krb5.keytab ]; then echo 'readable by current non-root user'; else echo 'not readable by current non-root user'; fi

fix.label: Rotate exposed keys
fix.text: If unauthorized users could read the keytab, restrict it immediately and rotate the affected Kerberos keys through the domain's supported enrollment process.

WIN-OS-BUILD.title: OS edition and build
WIN-OS-BUILD.why: The Windows edition, build, revision, and product type determine which security fixes and hardening features are available. Attackers use obsolete or unsupported builds to target known vulnerabilities with reliable exploits.

test.label: Show the operating-system build and product type

fix.label: Move to a supported build
fix.text: Apply the current servicing updates through Windows Update, WSUS, Configuration Manager, or your approved patch platform; upgrade the operating system if Microsoft no longer supports the reported release.

WIN-PATCH-AGE.title: Last update age
WIN-PATCH-AGE.semantics: FAIL: newest installed hotfix >90 days old; WARN: 45-90 days; PASS: <45; ERR: no hotfix dates readable.
WIN-PATCH-AGE.why: Old security updates leave publicly documented vulnerabilities available for exploitation, including flaws used for initial access and privilege escalation. The risk rises as exploit code and attacker tooling mature after disclosure.

test.label: Show the newest installed hotfix
test.cmd: Get-HotFix | Where-Object { $_.InstalledOn } | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 1 HotFixID,InstalledOn,Description

fix.label: Install current security updates
fix.text: Use Windows Update, WSUS, Configuration Manager, or the organization's approved patch platform to install applicable security and cumulative updates, then verify the newest installed update date.

WIN-FW-DOMAIN.title: Firewall - Domain profile
WIN-FW-DOMAIN.semantics: PASS: profile enabled (policy or local); WARN: disabled.
WIN-FW-DOMAIN.why: A disabled Domain firewall profile exposes listening services whenever the host authenticates to its domain network. An attacker with network access can probe those services and exploit weak authentication, unsafe configuration, or unpatched software.

fix.label: Enforce with Group Policy
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security > Windows Defender Firewall Properties > Domain Profile > Firewall state to On.

WIN-FW-PRIVATE.title: Firewall - Private profile
WIN-FW-PRIVATE.why: A disabled Private firewall profile exposes local services on networks that Windows classifies as trusted. A compromised device on the same network can scan and attack those services or attempt lateral movement.

fix.label: Enforce with Group Policy
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security > Windows Defender Firewall Properties > Private Profile > Firewall state to On.

WIN-FW-PUBLIC.title: Firewall - Public profile
WIN-FW-PUBLIC.why: A disabled Public firewall profile exposes the host on untrusted networks such as guest Wi-Fi. Nearby attackers can directly probe reachable services and exploit them without first entering the organization's trusted network.

fix.label: Enforce with Group Policy
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security > Windows Defender Firewall Properties > Public Profile > Firewall state to On.

WIN-DEF-RTP.title: Defender real-time protection
WIN-DEF-RTP.semantics: PASS: real-time protection on; FAIL: off; NA: Defender not present (third-party AV).
WIN-DEF-RTP.why: Without real-time antivirus protection, malicious files and processes may execute without being scanned at access or launch time. Attackers can use that gap to establish persistence, steal credentials, or deploy ransomware before a scheduled scan runs.

fix.label: Enforce with Group Policy
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Real-time Protection > Turn off real-time protection to Disabled, unless an approved third-party antivirus product replaces Defender.

WIN-DEF-TAMPER.title: Defender tamper protection
WIN-DEF-TAMPER.semantics: PASS: tamper protection on; WARN: off; NA: Defender not present.
WIN-DEF-TAMPER.why: Without tamper protection, malware or an intruder with sufficient local privileges can weaken Defender settings and exclusions. Disabling protection helps malicious activity persist and evade later detection.

fix.label: Enable tamper protection
fix.text: Enable Tamper protection in the Microsoft Defender portal, Microsoft Intune, or Windows Security according to the organization's management model; ordinary registry or PowerShell changes cannot reliably enable the protected setting.

WIN-DEF-SIGAGE.title: Defender signature age
WIN-DEF-SIGAGE.semantics: WARN: AV signatures >7 days old; PASS: <=7; NA: Defender not present.
WIN-DEF-SIGAGE.why: Stale antivirus intelligence may not recognize recently discovered malware families or updated payloads. Attackers deliberately modify known tools to evade old signatures and gain execution before cloud or behavioral controls intervene.

test.label: Show Defender signature age and update time

WIN-BITLOCKER.title: BitLocker on system drive
WIN-BITLOCKER.semantics: PASS: system drive protection on; WARN: off; ERR: not readable without elevation.
WIN-BITLOCKER.why: Without system-drive encryption, anyone who obtains the device or its disk can read files offline and bypass normal Windows access controls. The exposed material may include documents, cached credentials, browser data, and secrets used to reach other systems.

fix.label: Enable BitLocker with a TPM protector
Protect recovery material
fix.text: Back up the recovery password to the approved directory or device-management escrow before relying on BitLocker, and test the recovery process.

WIN-SECUREBOOT.title: UEFI Secure Boot
WIN-SECUREBOOT.semantics: PASS: UEFISecureBootEnabled=1; WARN: 0; INFO: legacy BIOS / state key absent.
WIN-SECUREBOOT.why: When Secure Boot is disabled, malicious or unauthorized boot components can execute before Windows security controls start. An attacker with firmware or physical access can use a bootkit to persist stealthily or tamper with the operating system.

test.label: Read the Secure Boot state recorded by Windows

fix.label: Enable UEFI Secure Boot
fix.text: Convert from legacy BIOS mode if necessary, enable UEFI and Secure Boot in the device firmware, and use vendor-supported signed boot components; suspend BitLocker and preserve its recovery key before firmware changes.

WIN-SMB-V1.title: SMBv1 server
WIN-SMB-V1.semantics: FAIL: SMB1 server enabled (LanmanServer SMB1=1 or mrxsmb10 driver enabled); PASS: disabled/absent.
WIN-SMB-V1.why: SMBv1 is an obsolete protocol with serious security weaknesses and a history of remotely exploitable flaws. An attacker can abuse an enabled SMBv1 server for compromise, downgrade opportunities, or rapid lateral propagation.

test.label: Inspect the SMB server protocol setting
Inspect the SMBv1 redirector driver state

WIN-SMB-SRVSIGN.title: SMB server signing required
WIN-SMB-SRVSIGN.why: If SMB server signing is not required, an attacker can relay captured authentication to the host and act with the victim's permissions. Signing binds SMB messages to the authenticated session and prevents an unsigned relay target from accepting the traffic.

test.label: Read the SMB server signing requirement

fix.label: Enforce with Group Policy
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always) to Enabled.

WIN-SMB-CLISIGN.title: SMB client signing required
WIN-SMB-CLISIGN.why: If SMB client signing is not required, an attacker can redirect or relay the client's authentication to an unsigned SMB service. This can expose credentials to relay attacks and allow manipulation of SMB traffic.

test.label: Read the SMB client signing requirement

fix.label: Enforce with Group Policy
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always) to Enabled.

WIN-NR-LLMNR.title: LLMNR
WIN-NR-LLMNR.semantics: FAIL: LLMNR not disabled by policy (DNSClient EnableMulticast!=0); PASS: 0.
WIN-NR-LLMNR.why: LLMNR allows local-link name-resolution responses when DNS resolution fails. An attacker on the same network can spoof a response, capture challenge-response credentials, and relay or crack them.

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn off multicast name resolution to Enabled.

WIN-NR-NBTNS.title: NetBIOS over TCP/IP
WIN-NR-NBTNS.semantics: WARN: >=1 IP-enabled adapter with NetBIOS not disabled (NetbiosOptions!=2); PASS: all disabled.
WIN-NR-NBTNS.why: NetBIOS name resolution permits unauthenticated local-network responses when modern name resolution does not provide an answer. An attacker can poison those responses to capture or relay Windows authentication.

test.label: Inspect NetBIOS settings on active adapters

fix.label: Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP on active adapters

WIN-NR-WPAD.title: WPAD auto-proxy discovery
WIN-NR-WPAD.semantics: WARN: WinHttpAutoProxySvc enabled and WPAD not disabled; PASS: service disabled or DisableWpad=1.
WIN-NR-WPAD.why: WPAD can cause a host to obtain proxy configuration from an attacker-controlled responder. A malicious proxy can intercept traffic, solicit Windows authentication, or relay captured credentials.

WIN-LDAP-CLISIGN.title: LDAP client signing
WIN-LDAP-CLISIGN.why: A client that does not require LDAP signing can establish LDAP sessions whose integrity is not protected. An attacker in a man-in-the-middle position can tamper with traffic or relay authentication to a permissive directory service.

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: LDAP client signing requirements to Require signing.

WIN-ANON-RESTRICT.title: Anonymous enumeration restrictions
WIN-ANON-RESTRICT.semantics: WARN: RestrictAnonymousSAM=0 or RestrictAnonymous=0 with EveryoneIncludesAnonymous=1; PASS: restricted.
WIN-ANON-RESTRICT.why: Weak anonymous-access restrictions can disclose account, group, share, or security-policy information without authentication. Attackers use that reconnaissance to identify privileged targets and prepare password attacks or lateral movement.

fix.label: Restrict anonymous enumeration
fix.cmd: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v RestrictAnonymousSAM /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f & reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v RestrictAnonymous /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f & reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v EveryoneIncludesAnonymous /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Use Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options to enable Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares and disable Network access: Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users.

WIN-PS-V2.title: PowerShell v2 engine
WIN-PS-V2.semantics: WARN: PowerShell 2.0 engine installed (downgrade bypasses logging); PASS: absent.
WIN-PS-V2.why: PowerShell 2.0 lacks modern script-block logging and other security improvements. An attacker can deliberately invoke the old engine to reduce telemetry and evade controls that depend on newer PowerShell features.

WIN-PS-SBLOG.title: PowerShell script-block logging
WIN-PS-SBLOG.semantics: PASS: EnableScriptBlockLogging=1 by policy; WARN: not enabled.
WIN-PS-SBLOG.why: Without script-block logging, PowerShell commands and decoded script content may be absent from forensic records. Attackers commonly use PowerShell for in-memory execution and obfuscation, making this telemetry important for detection and investigation.

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging to Enabled and forward the resulting event logs to protected storage.

WIN-PS-TRANSCRIPT.title: PowerShell transcription
WIN-PS-TRANSCRIPT.semantics: PASS: EnableTranscripting=1 by policy; WARN: not enabled.
WIN-PS-TRANSCRIPT.why: Without transcription, interactive PowerShell activity may leave limited human-readable evidence. An attacker can use administrative PowerShell sessions to alter the system while making reconstruction and accountability more difficult.

fix.label: Configure PowerShell transcription
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Transcription to Enabled and choose a secured, access-controlled output directory; protect transcripts because they may contain sensitive command output.

WIN-PS-LANGMODE.title: PowerShell language mode
WIN-PS-LANGMODE.semantics: INFO: current session language mode (FullLanguage / ConstrainedLanguage).
WIN-PS-LANGMODE.why: FullLanguage mode allows the current PowerShell session to access the complete language and .NET surface, while ConstrainedLanguage limits many capabilities when enforced by application control. Attackers who obtain PowerShell execution often prefer FullLanguage because it supports richer in-memory tooling and defense evasion.

test.label: Show the current session language mode

fix.label: Enforce application control where appropriate
fix.text: Deploy a tested Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker policy so untrusted PowerShell sessions enter ConstrainedLanguage mode; do not rely on manually changing the current session value as a security boundary.

WIN-RDP-ENABLED.title: Remote Desktop
WIN-RDP-ENABLED.why: An enabled Remote Desktop service adds a remotely reachable authentication and administration surface. Attackers can target it with password attacks, stolen credentials, or vulnerabilities, so its presence should match a documented operational requirement.

test.label: Read the Remote Desktop enable setting

fix.label: Disable Remote Desktop when unnecessary
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host > Connections > Allow users to connect remotely by using Remote Desktop Services to Disabled; otherwise restrict access with firewall rules, MFA-capable gateways, and authorized groups.

WIN-RDP-NLA.title: RDP Network Level Authentication
WIN-RDP-NLA.semantics: FAIL: RDP enabled and UserAuthentication!=1; PASS: NLA required; NA: RDP disabled.
WIN-RDP-NLA.why: Without Network Level Authentication, the host creates an RDP session before authenticating the user and exposes more of the service to unauthenticated clients. Attackers can consume resources, reach pre-authentication attack surface, and more easily conduct credential attacks.

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host > Security > Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication to Enabled.

WIN-CRED-RUNASPPL.title: LSA protection (RunAsPPL)
WIN-CRED-RUNASPPL.semantics: PASS: Lsa RunAsPPL 1 or 2; WARN: not set.
WIN-CRED-RUNASPPL.why: Without LSA protection, a sufficiently privileged malicious process can more easily inject into or read LSASS. Attackers target LSASS to recover reusable passwords, hashes, Kerberos material, and other credentials.

fix.label: Enable LSA protection with UEFI lock
Validate compatibility
fix.text: Audit LSA plug-ins and drivers for compatibility before broad deployment, then restart during an approved maintenance window and verify that protected-process logging reports no blocked production components.

WIN-CRED-CREDGUARD.title: Credential Guard
WIN-CRED-CREDGUARD.semantics: PASS: Credential Guard running; WARN: not running; ERR: DeviceGuard WMI unavailable.
WIN-CRED-CREDGUARD.why: Without Credential Guard, secrets used for domain authentication remain in the normal LSA environment and are more accessible after kernel or administrator-level compromise. Attackers can extract reusable credential material from LSASS and use it for lateral movement.

fix.label: Enable Credential Guard
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Guard > Turn On Virtualization Based Security and enable Credential Guard with the deployment's chosen UEFI-lock setting after validating hardware and application compatibility.

WIN-CRED-WDIGEST.title: WDigest cleartext credentials
WIN-CRED-WDIGEST.semantics: FAIL: WDigest UseLogonCredential=1 (cleartext passwords in LSASS); PASS: 0/absent on 8.1+.
WIN-CRED-WDIGEST.why: When WDigest credential caching is enabled, users' plaintext-equivalent passwords can remain in LSASS after logon. An attacker who gains sufficient local privileges can dump those credentials and reuse them across the environment.

WIN-CRED-LMCOMPAT.title: LAN Manager authentication level
WIN-CRED-LMCOMPAT.semantics: FAIL: LmCompatibilityLevel<3 (LM/NTLMv1 sent); WARN: 3-4 or unset; PASS: 5.
WIN-CRED-LMCOMPAT.why: Allowing LM or NTLMv1 authentication exposes weak challenge-response material that is practical to crack or relay. Attackers can force or capture legacy authentication and recover credentials for lateral movement.

test.label: Read the LAN Manager authentication level

fix.label: Require NTLMv2 and refuse LM and NTLM
Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: LAN Manager authentication level to Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM after testing legacy dependencies.

WIN-CRED-NOLMHASH.title: LM hash storage
WIN-CRED-NOLMHASH.why: Stored LM hashes are derived with obsolete, case-insensitive cryptography and can be cracked rapidly. An attacker who obtains the local account database or domain database can recover passwords more easily when LM hashes are retained.

fix.label: Prevent new LM hashes from being stored
Replace existing hashes
fix.text: After enabling the policy, require affected users to change their passwords because existing LM hashes are not removed until the corresponding password changes.

WIN-CRED-CACHEDLOGONS.title: Cached domain logons
WIN-CRED-CACHEDLOGONS.semantics: WARN: CachedLogonsCount >4 (default 10); PASS: <=4; NA: not domain-joined.
WIN-CRED-CACHEDLOGONS.why: Cached domain logons permit offline access but leave password-derived domain verifiers on the endpoint. An attacker who steals the system data can crack those verifiers offline, and a larger cache exposes more user accounts.

fix.label: Limit cached domain logons to four
Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache to the lowest value compatible with offline-use requirements.

WIN-UAC-LUA.title: UAC enabled
WIN-UAC-LUA.why: Disabling User Account Control causes administrative users and applications to run without normal elevation boundaries. Malware launched by an administrator can then modify protected system resources without an elevation prompt.

fix.label: Schedule the required restart
fix.text: Restart Windows during an approved maintenance window after changing EnableLUA, then verify application compatibility and the effective setting.

WIN-UAC-CONSENT.title: UAC admin consent prompt
WIN-UAC-CONSENT.semantics: WARN: ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0 (elevate without prompting); PASS: otherwise.
WIN-UAC-CONSENT.why: Elevating administrators without prompting removes an important warning and consent boundary. Code executing in an administrator's session can silently obtain a high-integrity token and make system-wide changes.

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode to a prompting option appropriate for the environment.

WIN-UAC-LATFP.title: LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy
WIN-UAC-LATFP.semantics: WARN: LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy=1 (full admin token for remote local-account logons; pass-the-hash); PASS: 0/absent.
WIN-UAC-LATFP.why: LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy=1 grants a full administrator token to remote network logons using local accounts. An attacker who obtains a local administrator hash can use pass-the-hash for unrestricted remote administration and lateral movement.

test.label: Read the remote local-account token policy

WIN-AIE.title: AlwaysInstallElevated
WIN-AIE.semantics: FAIL: AlwaysInstallElevated=1 in both HKLM and HKCU; PASS: otherwise.
WIN-AIE.why: When AlwaysInstallElevated is enabled for both the computer and current user, that user can install a crafted MSI package with SYSTEM privileges. An attacker who controls a nonadministrative account can use this configuration for immediate local privilege escalation.

fix.label: Disable both AlwaysInstallElevated policies
fix.cmd: reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" /v AlwaysInstallElevated /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f & reg add "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" /v AlwaysInstallElevated /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Always install with elevated privileges to Disabled under both Computer Configuration and User Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Installer.

WIN-ACCT-ADMINS.title: Local Administrators members
WIN-ACCT-ADMINS.semantics: INFO: member count and names of the local Administrators group.
WIN-ACCT-ADMINS.why: Every member of the local Administrators group can take full control of the host and access other users' data and credentials. Unexpected or excessive membership expands the set of accounts an attacker can compromise for local privilege escalation.

fix.label: Reduce administrator membership
fix.text: Remove unauthorized members, manage approved membership through restricted groups or Group Policy Preferences, and use Windows LAPS for the built-in local administrator rather than shared credentials.

WIN-ACCT-GUEST.title: Guest account
WIN-ACCT-GUEST.semantics: FAIL: built-in Guest enabled; PASS: disabled.
WIN-ACCT-GUEST.why: An enabled built-in Guest account provides a predictable local identity with deliberately limited authentication expectations. Attackers can use it for unauthorized access, reconnaissance, or interaction with resources that grant permissions to Guest or broad groups.

test.label: Inspect the built-in Guest account by SID

fix.label: Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Accounts: Guest account status to Disabled.

WIN-AUTOLOGON.title: AutoLogon stored password
WIN-AUTOLOGON.semantics: FAIL: Winlogon DefaultPassword present; WARN: AutoAdminLogon=1 without stored password; PASS: neither. Never prints the value.
WIN-AUTOLOGON.why: A DefaultPassword value stores an interactive logon password in a recoverable registry location, allowing local administrators and some remote management paths to obtain it. Even without a stored password, enabled automatic logon can grant physical users access to the configured account after startup.

test.label: Check AutoLogon state and password-value presence without reading the password

fix.label: Remove the stored password and disable AutoLogon
fix.cmd: Remove-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' -Name DefaultPassword -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' -Name AutoAdminLogon -Value '0'

WIN-LAPS.title: LAPS client policy
WIN-LAPS.semantics: PASS: Windows LAPS or legacy AdmPwd policy enabled; WARN: no LAPS policy; NA: not domain-joined.
WIN-LAPS.why: Without LAPS policy, local administrator passwords are often static or reused across domain computers. Compromise of one password can therefore enable pass-the-hash or password-based lateral movement to many hosts.

fix.label: Deploy Windows LAPS
fix.text: Configure Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > LAPS, set Configure password backup directory to Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID as appropriate, configure password settings, and delegate retrieval only to approved administrators.

WIN-SVC-SPOOLER.title: Print Spooler
WIN-SVC-SPOOLER.semantics: WARN: Spooler running on a domain controller (coercion/PrintNightmare surface); INFO: running on a non-DC; PASS: stopped/disabled.
WIN-SVC-SPOOLER.why: A running Print Spooler accepts complex print-related operations and has repeatedly exposed remote-code-execution and privilege-escalation paths. On a domain controller it also increases coercion risk because attackers may induce the DC to authenticate to another system.

test.label: Determine whether the host is a domain controller

fix.label: Stop and disable the Spooler where printing is unnecessary
Enforce with Group Policy
fix.text: For domain controllers and other systems that do not print, configure Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > System Services > Print Spooler with Disabled startup and stopped service state.

WIN-WINRM-HTTP.title: WinRM transport
WIN-WINRM-HTTP.semantics: FAIL: WinRM AllowUnencrypted=1; WARN: HTTP listener with no HTTPS listener; PASS: HTTPS or HTTP with encryption enforced; NA: WinRM not running.
WIN-WINRM-HTTP.why: AllowUnencrypted permits WinRM messages to be sent without transport-level message encryption when the selected authentication mechanism does not provide it. An HTTP-only listener also lacks TLS server authentication, increasing exposure to interception or impersonation even though normal Kerberos and NTLM sessions encrypt message content.

fix.label: Disallow unencrypted WinRM traffic
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Remote Management (WinRM) > WinRM Service > Allow unencrypted traffic to Disabled.

fix.label: Deploy HTTPS where transport authentication is required
fix.text: Provision a suitable server-authentication certificate and create a WinRM HTTPS listener; remove an unnecessary HTTP listener only after validating management connectivity.

WIN-DOMAIN-JOINED.title: Domain membership
WIN-DOMAIN-JOINED.semantics: INFO: domain name and role (workgroup / member / DC).
WIN-DOMAIN-JOINED.why: Domain membership and machine role determine which authentication paths, policies, and trust relationships apply to the host. Attackers value domain members for cached domain credentials and value domain controllers because compromise can expose directory-wide privileges.

fix.label: Validate the intended role
fix.text: Remove an unintended domain membership or domain-controller role through the organization's approved demotion or unjoin process; if membership is required, place the computer in the correct organizational unit and apply its security baseline.

AD-PWPOL-MINLEN.title: Domain minimum password length
AD-PWPOL-MINLEN.why: Short domain passwords have a smaller search space and are easier to guess online or crack after hashes are stolen. Compromising one domain account can provide initial access and a foothold for privilege escalation.

test.label: Read the default domain minimum length

fix.label: Set a minimum length of at least 14
Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Edit the domain password policy at Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy > Minimum password length; also assess fine-grained password policies that may override the default for particular users.

AD-PWPOL-LOCKOUT.title: Domain account lockout threshold
AD-PWPOL-LOCKOUT.why: A zero lockout threshold permits unlimited online password guesses, while a very high threshold gives attackers many attempts per account. A measured threshold slows password attacks, though monitoring and protections against lockout denial-of-service remain necessary.

test.label: Read the default domain lockout policy

fix.label: Set the default threshold to ten attempts
Configure Group Policy
fix.text: Edit Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy and select a threshold from 1 through 10 with suitable duration and reset values; review fine-grained password policies separately.

AD-PWPOL-MAXAGE.title: Domain maximum password age
AD-PWPOL-MAXAGE.semantics: INFO: maxPwdAge in days (0 = never expires).
AD-PWPOL-MAXAGE.why: Maximum password age describes how long the default domain policy permits a password to remain unchanged, with zero meaning no forced expiration. Excessive rotation can encourage predictable passwords, while non-expiring passwords increase exposure when credentials are compromised and no risk-based reset occurs.

test.label: Read the default domain maximum password age

fix.label: Align expiration with the identity policy
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy > Maximum password age according to the organization's risk-based standard, and prioritize MFA, compromised-password screening, and immediate resets after suspected compromise.

AD-KRBTGT-AGE.title: krbtgt password age
AD-KRBTGT-AGE.semantics: FAIL: krbtgt pwdLastSet >365 days; WARN: 180-365; PASS: <180.
AD-KRBTGT-AGE.why: The krbtgt account protects Kerberos ticket-granting tickets for the domain, so an old password increases the period during which stolen key material may remain useful. An attacker with the krbtgt key can forge Golden Tickets and impersonate highly privileged users.

test.label: Show the krbtgt password-set date and age

fix.label: Rotate krbtgt safely
fix.text: Follow Microsoft's krbtgt recovery procedure: verify replication health, reset the password once, allow replication and existing ticket lifetimes to pass, then reset it a second time; coordinate the operation as a domain-wide change.

AD-KERBEROASTABLE.title: Kerberoastable user accounts
AD-KERBEROASTABLE.semantics: FAIL: >=1 enabled user (not computer) with an SPN; PASS: 0.
AD-KERBEROASTABLE.why: Any authenticated domain user can request a service ticket for an enabled user account that has an SPN. An attacker can extract the ticket's password-derived ciphertext and crack it offline, potentially recovering a service account password with elevated access.

test.label: List enabled noncomputer users with SPNs

fix.label: Harden SPN-bearing user accounts
fix.text: Remove obsolete SPNs and accounts, migrate supported services to group Managed Service Accounts, assign long randomly generated passwords to remaining service users, minimize their privileges, and rotate exposed credentials.

AD-ASREP.title: AS-REP roastable accounts
AD-ASREP.semantics: FAIL: >=1 enabled account with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH; PASS: 0.
AD-ASREP.why: Accounts that do not require Kerberos preauthentication allow anyone to request password-derived AS-REP material without knowing the password. An attacker can crack that material offline and use the recovered credentials for domain access.

test.label: List enabled accounts that do not require preauthentication

fix.label: Rotate exposed credentials
fix.text: After reenabling preauthentication, reset the account password to a strong random value and investigate whether the account's AS-REP material was previously collected.

AD-UNCONSTRAINED.title: Unconstrained delegation (non-DC)
AD-UNCONSTRAINED.semantics: FAIL: >=1 enabled non-DC computer or user with TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION; PASS: 0.
AD-UNCONSTRAINED.why: Unconstrained delegation allows delegated accounts or computers to retain users' forwardable Kerberos ticket-granting tickets. An attacker who compromises such a non-DC system can capture privileged tickets and impersonate their owners across the domain.

test.label: List enabled non-DC principals trusted for unconstrained delegation

fix.label: Use constrained delegation
fix.text: Where delegation is required, redesign the service for resource-based constrained delegation or constrained delegation with protocol transition only when necessary, and protect privileged accounts from delegation.

AD-ADMINCOUNT.title: adminCount=1 users
AD-ADMINCOUNT.semantics: INFO: count of users with adminCount=1.
AD-ADMINCOUNT.why: adminCount=1 identifies users that are or were subject to AdminSDHolder protection, including accounts that may once have held privileged group membership. A large or unexpected population can reveal privilege sprawl, stale protected ACLs, and attractive attacker targets.

fix.label: Review protected-account history
fix.text: Confirm each account's current privileged memberships, remove obsolete privilege, and remediate stale adminCount and ACL inheritance only after verifying that the account is no longer protected by AdminSDHolder.

AD-DA-MEMBERS.title: Domain Admins membership
AD-DA-MEMBERS.semantics: WARN: >5 distinct (recursive) members; INFO: count otherwise.
AD-DA-MEMBERS.why: Domain Admins members can control domain controllers, directory policy, and nearly every domain identity. Excessive membership gives attackers more accounts to phish, steal, or misuse for complete domain compromise.

test.label: List recursive Domain Admins membership by well-known SID

fix.label: Reduce Domain Admins membership
fix.text: Remove accounts that do not require persistent domain-wide control, use separate privileged identities and time-bound elevation for administrative work, and alert on every membership change.

AD-PROTECTED-USERS.title: Protected Users group
AD-PROTECTED-USERS.semantics: WARN: Protected Users has no members; PASS: >=1.
AD-PROTECTED-USERS.why: Protected Users applies additional credential protections to suitable high-value domain accounts, including restrictions on legacy authentication and credential caching. If the group is empty, no eligible privileged account receives those safeguards against credential theft and reuse.

test.label: List Protected Users membership by well-known SID

fix.label: Add compatible privileged users
fix.text: After testing authentication and delegation dependencies, add suitable human privileged accounts to Protected Users; do not add service accounts or accounts that require NTLM, DES, delegation, or long-lived Kerberos tickets.

AD-MAQ.title: Machine account quota
AD-MAQ.semantics: WARN: ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota>0 (any user can join computers; RBCD/Certifried aid); PASS: 0.
AD-MAQ.why: A positive machine-account quota lets ordinary authenticated users create computer accounts in the domain. Attackers can abuse those accounts in resource-based constrained delegation, certificate-service attack chains, or other identity-manipulation techniques.

fix.label: Set the machine-account quota to zero
Delegate joins explicitly
fix.text: Grant computer-creation or domain-join rights only to a controlled provisioning identity or approved administrators in the required organizational units.

AD-FUNC-LEVEL.title: Domain/forest functional level
AD-FUNC-LEVEL.semantics: WARN: domain functional level below 2016 (msDS-Behavior-Version<7); PASS: >=7.
AD-FUNC-LEVEL.why: Older domain functional levels retain compatibility with obsolete domain-controller generations and prevent use of newer directory capabilities. Attackers benefit when legacy protocols, systems, and weaker security assumptions must remain supported.

test.label: Read numeric domain and forest behavior versions
Show friendly functional-level names
test.cmd: Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot,DomainMode; Get-ADForest | Select-Object RootDomain,ForestMode

fix.label: Raise functional levels after validation
fix.text: Remove or upgrade unsupported domain controllers, verify replication and application compatibility, then use Active Directory Domains and Trusts or Set-ADDomainMode and Set-ADForestMode to raise the levels; treat this as a planned, forest-wide change.

AD-LDAP-SIGNING.title: DC LDAP signing / channel binding
AD-LDAP-SIGNING.semantics: Run on a DC. FAIL: LDAPServerIntegrity<2, or signing required but LdapEnforceChannelBinding unset/0 (LDAPS relay open); WARN: channel binding 1 (when supported); PASS: LDAPServerIntegrity=2 AND LdapEnforceChannelBinding=2; NA: not a DC observer; ERR: registry unreadable (never a false PASS).
AD-LDAP-SIGNING.why: A domain controller that does not require LDAP signing can accept integrity-unprotected LDAP binds. An attacker can relay authentication to LDAP or alter traffic and then make directory changes with the relayed user's permissions. Signing alone does not stop relay to LDAPS: without channel binding (LdapEnforceChannelBinding=2) a relayed NTLM bind over TLS is still accepted.

test.label: Read LDAP signing enforcement locally on each domain controller
Read LDAP channel-binding enforcement on each domain controller

fix.label: Configure the domain-controller GPO
fix.text: Set Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements to Require signing, and test legacy LDAP clients before enforcement.

fix.label: Always enforce LDAP channel binding (after auditing clients with event 3039)

AD-TRUSTS.title: Domain trusts
AD-TRUSTS.semantics: INFO: count and direction of trustedDomain objects.
AD-TRUSTS.why: Domain and forest trusts extend authentication and authorization paths across security boundaries. An obsolete, overly broad, or poorly monitored trust can let an attacker pivot from a compromised trusted domain or abuse cross-domain identities.

test.label: List domain trusts and their direction

fix.label: Review and constrain trusts
fix.text: Remove trusts with no current business owner, prefer one-way direction and selective authentication where feasible, enable appropriate SID filtering, and monitor changes and cross-trust authentication.

AD-LAPS-SCHEMA.title: LAPS schema present
AD-LAPS-SCHEMA.semantics: PASS: ms-Mcs-AdmPwd or msLAPS-Password attribute in schema; WARN: neither.
AD-LAPS-SCHEMA.why: Without Windows LAPS or legacy Microsoft LAPS schema attributes, Active Directory cannot store the managed local-administrator password data required by those deployments. Organizations may then fall back to static or reused local passwords that enable broad lateral movement after one endpoint is compromised.

test.label: Search the schema for Windows or legacy LAPS password attributes

fix.label: Extend the schema for Windows LAPS
Complete the deployment
fix.text: After extending the schema, delegate computer self-update and password-retrieval permissions, configure the Windows LAPS policy, and audit which principals can read password attributes.
